headline: Stop Asking ChatGPT Wrong: Prompt Patterns That Work
summary: Most developers treat LLMs like search engines, but they're reasoning engines. This carousel reveals the prompt architecture patterns that turn unreliable outputs into production-grade code generation.

slides.title: You're Using LLMs Like Search Engines
slides.subtitle: LLMs are reasoning engines, not lookup tables
slides.body: Developers paste vague requests and expect perfect code. The model has no context of your codebase, constraints, or standards. Result: hallucinated APIs, wrong patterns, wasted review time.
slides.deep_dive: Large language models predict next tokens based on statistical patterns in training data. They don't 'know' your stack, your conventions, or your business logic. When you ask 'write a REST API,' the model averages every REST tutorial it saw — not your team's middleware, error handling, or auth strategy. The gap between average training output and your production requirements is where bugs live.
slides.key_fact: LLMs generate probable continuations, not verified solutions
slides.why_it_matters: Treating generation as retrieval creates technical debt you'll debug for weeks

slides.title: How LLMs Actually Process Your Prompt
slides.subtitle: Context window → Attention → Next-token prediction
slides.body: Your prompt assembles a temporary 'working memory.' The model attends to relevant parts, then predicts tokens sequentially. No internal verification loop exists.
slides.deep_dive: Think of the context window as a whiteboard. Everything you write — instructions, examples, code snippets — gets written on that board. The model's attention mechanism highlights relevant sections as it generates each token. But there's no 'check your work' phase. Once a token is emitted, it conditions all future tokens. Early errors compound. This is why structure matters: you're not querying a database; you're setting up initial conditions for a generative process.
slides.key_fact: No built-in verification — output quality equals prompt structure quality
slides.why_it_matters: Prompt design is initial-condition engineering for a stochastic process

slides.title: Prompt Anatomy: Input → Transformation → Output
slides.subtitle: Structure determines whether reasoning activates
slides.body: Role + Context + Constraints + Examples + Task = Reliable reasoning trigger. Missing pieces default to training averages.
slides.deep_dive: A well-structured prompt acts like a function signature with preconditions. The role sets the persona (senior engineer, security reviewer). Context provides the 'global state' (tech stack, existing patterns). Constraints define postconditions (no external deps, follow style guide). Examples demonstrate the input-output mapping — this is few-shot priming. The task is the actual call. When all five align, the model's attention focuses on relevant training subspaces. Omit any, and the model fills gaps with statistical averages — which rarely match your reality.
slides.key_fact: Five-component structure activates task-specific reasoning pathways
slides.why_it_matters: Each missing component increases variance exponentially
slides.processing: Attention focuses on relevant training subspaces

slides.title: Prompt Patterns: Latency vs Reliability Trade-offs
slides.subtitle: More context = better output but higher cost and latency
slides.body: Zero-shot is fast but brittle. Few-shot adds tokens but anchors behavior. Chain-of-thought adds reasoning tokens but catches errors early.
slides.deep_dive: Zero-shot: single prompt, lowest latency, highest variance. Good for exploration, bad for production. Few-shot: 3-5 examples consume context window but dramatically reduce output variance — the model learns the pattern in-context. Chain-of-thought: explicit reasoning steps ('think step by step') add generation tokens but expose logic errors before code emits. Self-consistency: multiple CoT runs with majority vote — highest reliability, 3-5x latency. Structured output (JSON schema): constrains format, enables parsing, slight token overhead. Choose based on failure cost: prototype → zero-shot; production API → few-shot + schema; critical logic → CoT + self-consistency.
slides.key_fact: Reliability scales with context investment — no free lunch
slides.why_it_matters: Match pattern to failure cost: prototype vs production vs safety-critical

slides.title: Vague Prompts vs Structured Prompts
slides.subtitle: The difference between 'write code' and 'write this specific code'
slides.body: Naive prompts omit role, context, constraints, examples. Result: generic training averages. Structured prompts specify every dimension.
slides.deep_dive: The naive prompt 'Write a Python function to parse JSON' yields a textbook example — no error handling, no typing, no logging, no validation. The structured prompt specifies: 'You are a senior Python engineer. Our codebase uses Pydantic v2, structlog, and custom exceptions. Write a parse_json function that validates against a schema, logs parsing errors with correlation IDs, and raises our ValidationError. Here are 3 examples from our codebase.' The second prompt activates the 'senior engineer with our stack' subspace. The first activates 'average Python tutorial.' Same model, wildly different outputs.
slides.key_fact: Unspecified dimensions default to training-set averages
slides.why_it_matters: Every omitted constraint becomes a review-cycle bug

slides.title: How Teams Build Prompt Pipelines, Not One-offs
slides.subtitle: Versioned prompts + automated eval + CI gates = reliable generation
slides.body: High-throughput teams treat prompts as code: versioned, tested, evaluated, gated. Not chat history — engineered artifacts.
slides.deep_dive: Production prompt engineering mirrors software engineering. Prompts live in version control with semantic versioning. Automated evaluation suites run on every change — unit tests for generation (schema validity, style compliance), integration tests (does the code compile, pass lint, run?). CI gates block merges if eval scores regress. A/B testing compares prompt versions on real tasks. Observability tracks latency, token cost, error rates per prompt version. Rollback is instant. This transforms prompting from art to engineering discipline. The prompt becomes a deterministic component in your build pipeline, not a chat session.
slides.key_fact: Prompts become versioned, tested, observable pipeline components
slides.why_it_matters: Eliminates 'works on my chat' syndrome; enables team collaboration

slides.title: Start These Three Habits Today
slides.subtitle: Small prompt investments compound into massive review-time savings
slides.body: Adopt structured prompts, few-shot examples, and eval gates. Your future self — and your reviewers — will thank you.
slides.deep_dive: The highest-leverage change is adding 3 curated examples to every generation task. This alone shifts output from 'average tutorial' to 'your codebase pattern.' Next, define a prompt template with role, context, constraints — reuse it. Finally, add one eval check: does generated code pass your linter? That single gate catches 80% of hallucinated APIs. Build from there. Prompt engineering isn't prompt writing — it's prompt lifecycle management.
slides.key_fact: Three examples + one eval gate = 80% hallucination reduction
slides.why_it_matters: Compound interest on prompt quality pays in saved review cycles
takeaways: Add 3 curated examples matching your codebase patterns to every generation prompt
Create a reusable prompt template with role, context, constraints — version it
Gate generation with at least one automated check (lint, type-check, schema validation)
